title: Teen who singer D4vd is accused of killing had multiple abortions, texts reveal
description: WARNING: Readers may find details in this article distressing.Texts between singer D4vd and Celeste Rivas Hernandez, the 14-year-old he is accused of
body: WARNING: Readers may find details in this article distressing.Texts between singer D4vd and Celeste Rivas Hernandez, the 14-year-old he is accused of murdering, reveal she had been pregnant and had had an abortion before her death. The messages were shown during a hearing for a judge to determine if the singer, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, should go on trial for the teen's death last year."What [if] the first abortion didn't work?" Celeste texted Burke in June 2024, according to prosecutors. She was 13 years old at the time and he was 19. Prosecutors say Burke killed her after she threatened to reveal he had been abusing a minor and destroy his career. He has pleaded not guilty to charges of murdering and sexually abusing the girl.In an exchange from January 2024, Burke apologised to the teen for "putting her through this", according to messages shown in the Los Angeles court on Friday.She responded, "neither of us are capable of watching and taking care of the baby. it's for the best no?"Burke asked, "also my mother always told me to ask this question if I was ever in this situation … it is mine right?" Celeste replied "of course its yours David", according to testimony from a detective.The court heard that in another text to the teen, sent in June 2024, Burke wrote: "Let's let this abortion be the last one til we have the real one…" Prosecutors presented iCloud data recovered from the defendant's iPhone, showing texts between him and Celeste dating back to 8 August 2022, when she was 11 years old and he was 17.The device belonging to Burke also had photos of the teenager during the alleged sexual abuse, prosecutors and Los Angeles Police Detective Corey Farell said on Friday.The victim's mother, Mercedes Rivas Hernandez, became visibly emotional and left the court with her husband as details of some of the pictures were described during the proceedings. Burke's phone also showed conversations the two had had about moving in together, which they had dubbed "Operation Awesome".The pair "broke up" in November 2024, but stayed in contact, according to a memo filed by prosecutors earlier this year. Prosecutors allege they argued on the night before her death, allegedly over Burke's relationships with other women.Dr Grant Ho of the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner, who conducted the post-mortem examination on Celeste, also testified on Friday.Ho told the court it was "extremely difficult to tell" exactly when the girl died, owing to the state of decomposition when her remains were found.Lawyers for the defence seized on that uncertainty, questioning whether it was possible that the teenager could have somehow harmed herself. Farrell, the police detective, testified that DNA taken from blood found in Burke's Hollywood Hills home and garage was a match for Celeste.D4vd, who rose to fame on TikTok with the viral hits Romantic Homicide and Here With Me, was on tour when police found Celeste's body in the front boot of his Tesla in September 2025 - the day after she would have turned 15. His worldwide tour was cancelled and he largely retreated from public life and social media.Police announced his arrest in April this year.Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman has filed seven criminal charges against him, including murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child and the mutilation of remains.They said the teen was reported missing by her family and was last seen at Burke's home on 3 April 2025 - five months before her remains were discovered in the Tesla.Prosecutors have said he met Celeste online when she was 11, and allege he started sexually abusing her when she was 13 and he was 18. Friday marked the fourth day of testimony in the pre-trial hearing. Earlier revelations by prosecutors included that Hernandez had been brought by Burke to London and Texas to meet members of his family there. Testimony is expected to resume on Monday.

schema.headline: Teen who singer D4vd is accused of killing had multiple abortions, texts reveal

title: Trump takes swipes at press during White House Correspondents' Dinner
description: In her remarks, WHCA President Weijia Jiang of CBS News said the event would return to the scene of the April shooting, the Washington Hilton, next ye
body: In her remarks, WHCA President Weijia Jiang of CBS News said the event would return to the scene of the April shooting, the Washington Hilton, next year.The officer shot at the scene, officer Victor Gonzalez of the US Secret Service, was given an award by Trump for his actions on the night of the shooting.Trump stood and shook hands with award winners, including a Wall Street Journal team who was given an award for coverage of Trump's links to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.Ahead of the event, many in the White House press corps theorised that Trump - who often criticises many of the reporters seated just metres away in the room - would deliver a stern rebuke of the media.In his remarks, Trump was at times cordial and conciliatory, saying "the second time is always better", joking and praising the media - saying he respects "most of them"."As I said three months ago, the show must go on," Trump said.But there were also some pointed insults directed at several journalists, some of whom were in the room. The harsher tone and personal attacks extended to Democratic politicians and celebrities as his hour-long speech took aim at some familiar targets.The US president also called on Americans to respect freedom of speech."We settle our differences not with bullets, but with open and vigorous debate," Trump said. "And no deranged loser with a gun will ever change that. We can't let that ever happen."Trump appeared to be in a good mood throughout the event, jokingly telling the media that "sometimes I really do think that some of you don't like me"."This place [the dinner] is really the largest group of 'Trump derangement syndrome' people ever put together at one time," he said. "I suspect some of you are lucky that our last dinner was cut short...I was going to go after you."The president joked the news industry would "be broke" after he is no longer in office because "there's not going to be anybody to report on", before putting on a Trump 2028 hat and saying he would run for another term.The gala dinner came as relations between the White House and the media remain fraught. Last week, Trump threatened to revoke the licences of several US networks which did not carry his primetime speech about election security. The event was considerably scaled down from the first correspondents' dinner, with about 700 people in attendance, compared with more than 2,000 in April.Security was also tighter. Several blocks around the hotel were blocked off, with a heavy presence of police and national guard. Guests were screened twice, with QR codes and IDs, and were given wristbands.At one point, visitors were prompted to walk in a single file line past two Secret Service officers holding rifles.The suspect of the shooting in April, identified as 31-year-old Cole Tomas Allen, has been charged with attempting to assassinate the president of the United States. He was tackled by agents just short of a staircase which leads down to a ballroom where the dinner was getting underway.Others in attendance on Saturday night included Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

schema.headline: Trump takes swipes at press during White House Correspondents' Dinner

title: Jermain Defoe: Growing concerns before exit - Woking sporting director
description: Woking director of football Jody Brown says there were "growing concerns" across the club before the National League side parted ways with former Engl
body: Woking director of football Jody Brown says there were "growing concerns" across the club before the National League side parted ways with former England striker Jermain Defoe as manager.The two parties "mutually agreed to part ways with immediate effect" earlier this week, with the 43-year-old Defoe having been in charge for just four months and six league games.His exit came two weeks before Woking's opening match of the new season against Sutton United."Jermain's feedback was always positive, and he regularly expressed his enthusiasm and excitement for the season, both publicly and privately," said Brown., external"I can therefore appreciate the surprise and subsequent speculation surrounding his sudden departure."However, in recent weeks there had been feedback from across the club, including players, staff and other departments, regarding growing concerns."Brown said that led him to ask Defoe and assistant Paul Bracewell for a brief report "outlining the squad's current depth, recruitment targets and any operational challenges" so he could provide the "support required" but, despite requesting it more than once, it "was never received"."A meeting was subsequently scheduled involving the directors, manager, assistant manager and head of operations to review preparations for the season," he added."Neither Jermain nor his assistant attended that meeting or that day's training session."Throughout his tenure, Jermain had never communicated any serious concerns directly to me, so I am not going to speculate on his reasons."Defoe scored 305 goals in 763 senior appearances for clubs including West Ham, Tottenham, Portsmouth and Sunderland, while scoring 20 times in 57 international appearances, before retiring in 2022.He was part of an interim coaching staff at Rangers in 2021 and worked in the Spurs academy, before leaving in 2024 to pursue a full-time managerial role.Defoe said his stint at Woking had been "an eye-opening managerial experience and one that will undoubtedly make me stronger for the next challenge in my career".Brown took responsibility for appointing the "likeable" Defoe as he "believed he was the right person to lead the club into an exciting new era".But he said: "As we have seen many times before, success as a player does not always translate into management and leadership. I sincerely hope to see him succeed in whichever direction he follows."

schema.headline: Jermain Defoe: Growing concerns before exit - Woking sporting director

title: Five ways to make the most of the summer holidays with kids
description: Image source, Nilly DahliaImage caption, Nilly Dahlia says she wants her kids to enjoy a "nostalgic summer"ByEmily HoltThe six-week summer holidays ha
body: Image source, Nilly DahliaImage caption, Nilly Dahlia says she wants her kids to enjoy a "nostalgic summer"ByEmily HoltThe six-week summer holidays have officially begun and, for many parents, finding exciting but affordable activities for children can be tough. For most families in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the break is already under way. In Scotland, children have enjoyed some time off already, but will return to school earlier than those elsewhere in the UK.Here are five tips to help children get the most out of the next few weeks of summer. 1. Not every holiday has to be abroad A family's first instinct when summer is approaching may be to look at booking a trip abroad, but rising costs and travel expenses mean a holiday isn't feasible for everyone. Mags Rivett, director at Family Holiday Charity, which supports families with UK trips, says there are many benefits to arranging time away with children that don't require expensive travel. She says the social aspect of a holiday can help children develop their communication skills. "Lots of kids have never really had the opportunity to meet people outside of their own community," Rivett says. "But if you go somewhere that's got social facilities, it's a really important opportunity."She says getting recommendations from friends and family is a good place to start. Rivett gives the example of Skegness, a coastal holiday destination in Lincolnshire, accessible by train or coach, which her charity has supported families to visit.A family-of-four's accommodation in a holiday park there this August starts at around £750 for a week, while an off-peak return train from Manchester would cost around £280 for four.By contrast, a last-minute trip to Majorca for a family-of-four at that time starts from around £2,000. Better deals can usually be found booking further in advance.2. Prioritise the moments, not the cost Samantha Thomas, creator of Budget Mum UK, says she focuses on the time she can give her children, rather than the money she could spend on a day out. Thomas suggests focusing on your budget first to understand what you can comfortably spend, and then build your activities around that, to help remove any "stress or guilt" during the holidays. "Children don't need a six-week programme of expensive activities," Thomas says. "Some of the memories that they'll treasure most will come from simple things, like baking together or a picnic in the park, or building a den in the living room."Ingredients to bake fairy cakes with buttercream icing usually cost between £10 and £15 - depending on what you already have in the cupboard.For a picnic - or picky bits - prices can vary. But it can easily be done on a budget of around £5. Image source, Samantha ThomasImage caption, Samantha Thomas says treasured family memories can be created on a budgetTasneem Abdur-Rashid, an author and single mum of two, echoes Thomas' opinion and wants to relieve the pressure she puts on herself to do something different with her children every day. She says it's important to take time out, put work away, and spend one-on-one time with your children. This could be going to play in the park, or going swimming.Trips to local pools or lidos can cost around £6 for adults, and £3.50 for children.Abdur-Rashid says every night during the holidays she will play board games with her children, which blends quality time and fun. These can be picked up at local charity shops for very reasonable prices."You don't even have to leave the house for that," she says, "and they love it."3. Use what's available in your area Nilly Dahlia, a content creator and mum of three, says she prints out a six-week calendar with a range of activities for her kids during the holidays. As part of their "summer bucket list", they are planning to check out all the parks in the local area and she is prioritising low-cost activities throughout the summer. "I feel like there's this intense pressure to have Instagram-worthy holidays now," she says."What's wrong with just staying in the UK, staying out till sunset, riding your bike, just going to the river, like I did? I really want the kids to experience a nostalgic summer."Dahlia stresses there are many things on offer during the holidays that won't break the bank, such as free kids' meals in cafes and discounts on local travel. And there are often offers at bowling venues and cinemas, she says, while her family enjoys a movie night at home every Friday."They each have a bowl of popcorn and treats and we move the sofas into two rows so it's like a cinema."James Gray, communications and advocacy manager at Libraries Connected, says the summer holidays are also where libraries "come alive". He says libraries across the UK will hold the Summer Reading Challenge, encouraging kids to read more in a fun format, and many will be hosting events such as arts and crafts, performances and creative workshops, all for free. 4. Balance rest with some learningDahlia says she picks up books for her children to get them ready for the next school year. Her youngest will receive some chapter books to help them transition into Year 3, while her eldest is moving to secondary school, and Dahlia has prepped suitable books to bridge that gap from primary.She preps "summer baskets" which include puzzle books, reading books and snacks  to curb any boredom. "It's so important because by reading, they're still engaging their brain so they can go back to school in September, already having vocabulary in them."As a busy parent, Abdur-Rashid says she doesn't always have the time to do everything she'd like with her children, but structures their days to make sure they are always doing an activity. She allocates an hour a day for gaming which her boys enjoy, and then fills the rest of the time with playing, reading or writing. She also wants to foster a passion for reading in her kids, and allows them to not finish books they don't enjoy so reading doesn't become a "punishment".Image source, Tasneem Abdur-RashidImage caption, Author Tasneem Abdur-Rashid suggests parks and picnics for low-cost quality time with your childrenGavin Morgan, an education psychologist at University College London, says it's important to let children be "bored" during the holidays. "It's really important that they have opportunities to switch off from school and from that structure in order to experience and explore new things and get bored, because for some kids, that can really spark that creativity."For those entering exam years, Morgan says parents should have a conversation with their child about what they need to do and what suits them best. "The worst thing for parents to do is put their child under any kind of pressure, because they'll end up being switched off from learning," he says.He says parents should encourage their children to take a break from their education, so they return to school in September "feeling really confident and refreshed".5. Get ahead for the next holidays Thomas says she starts planning her summer budget well in advance. She does this by contributing a little bit of money every month into a "sinking fund" - a pot of money set aside for a specific purpose.This summer her budget is £500, and she sits down with her children to discuss how much they have budgeted and to brainstorm activities they can do together. "You've got that open dialogue, so they understand there's only a finite amount of money, and we've got a plan on how to do that best," she says.Thomas also uses cashback websites to get money back on things she has bought, which she says is "brilliant for hotels or travel". If you are planning a holiday, whether abroad or in the UK, Thomas stresses to plan and book in advance to get better deals. She also recommends looking at attractions within your local area before travelling further afield. Additional reporting by Hayley Clarke

schema.headline: Five ways to make the most of the summer holidays with kids

title: Ukraine's Zelensky struggles to fix crisis over removal of defence minister Fedorov
description: With an acting defence minister in place and a new commander-in-chief in charge of the military, Ukraine's recent political crisis is over, right?Not
body: With an acting defence minister in place and a new commander-in-chief in charge of the military, Ukraine's recent political crisis is over, right?Not so fast.The political fallout from President Volodymyr Zelensky's 15 July decision not to re-appoint Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister, as part of a cabinet reshuffle, continues to reverberate about Kyiv and beyond, even as air raid sirens wail and Russian drones and missiles are intercepted overhead.Fedorov's mostly young supporters are still mounting daily street protests, demanding that Zelensky reinstate the popular young innovator widely credited with driving much of Ukraine's recent technological innovation.On Thursday, Fedorov said he had rejected Zelensky's offers of alternative posts in government, saying there were only three positions worth having to influence the course of the war: minister of defence, commander-in-chief of the military or president of Ukraine."If you don't have a ministry under you, you don't have a budget," ex-deputy defence minister Alina Frolova said, "and you don't actually have the authority to do something."Fedorov's reference to the presidency did not go unnoticed. Was this the first public sign that the ousted minister sees himself as a rival to Zelensky?One former defence official suggested he became a real candidate for the presidency the moment he was dismissed.But with the country at war and no elections scheduled – Ukraine's constitution still prevents them in wartime – how useful is it to put your head above the political parapet so far in advance?"He's being childish," one opposition MP told me, on condition that he remained anonymous."He's looking to further his political career, which I think is just stupid in the circumstances where we are."The president's supporters say Zelensky has gone to great lengths to resolve the crisis, especially over the question of who to replace the unpopular commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi.Eventually he decided on Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43, a highly respected former commander of Ukraine's land forces."He consulted pretty much every significant figure in the Ukrainian army," former government adviser Yuriy Sak told the BBC earlier this week."So the decision that he has taken now is very well informed, and I support it because General Drapatyi is a young, battle-proven, modern general who will take our defences to a new level, hopefully."But while Drapatyi's appointment has been generally welcomed, it only represents a partial fix by a president scrambling to repair the damage caused by his removal of Fedorov.Ironically, for a president whose youth and apparent dynamism propelled him to power in 2019, Zelensky seems to have misjudged the mood of young Ukrainians, eager for their leaders – political and military – to represent their values and aspirations."It's quite natural that people want to see someone who is a warrior against corruption, who is very modern, who is young," Oleksandr Merezhko, an MP from Zelensky's Servant of the People party, said."People want to see something like that in politics, which they consider to be dirty and full of hypocrisy. They need heroes."But Merezhko agrees that Fedorov's ambitions and almost mythic, popular status may have brought about his downfall, especially for a president with a track record of sidelining those he sees as potential rivals."Don't outshine your master," Merezhko says, quoting from Robert Greene's 1998 self-help book, The 48 Laws of Power.Most analysts agree that last week's reshuffle had one overarching purpose: to cut Fedorov down to size. But Zelensky's strategy appears to have backfired."His removal has led to the opposite result," Merezhko says. "His rating soared. Just soared."Few doubt Fedorov's commitment, imagination and drive, but some question whether his outsized reputation is fully justified.They point out that he inherited a situation in which Ukraine had already successfully built up its medium- and long-range strike capabilities, something over which the defence minister has little day-to-day influence."The energy and clarity he brought to the job was impressive and he showed immense personal courage," a former European defence official said. "But the thing that will carry on regardless is the innovation culture. It's 2,000 companies, not a single individual."One opposition MP, who asked not to be identified, put it more bluntly."Ninety-nine per cent of these young people on the street have no clue how the ministry of defence is operating, how the general staff is operating," he said."They think Fedorov is good because he wants to fight with drones and Syrskyi was bad because he was looking for people to fight. It's a dramatic simplification which is totally wrong."But understandable, perhaps, in a country exhausted by 12 years of war with Russia. Who would not want to believe that drones and robots can do the job, rather than a member of your own family, roughly conscripted on the streets of your own hometown?Everyone agrees that Ukraine needs to put this politically toxic episode behind it before summer gives way to autumn and the country braces itself for another Russian assault on its energy grid."We need to prepare for how we will get through the winter," Zelensky said on the Telegram messaging app on Thursday.Politicians and experts interviewed for this piece mostly agree that while the political damage of this episode continues to undermine President Zelensky's authority and reputation, Ukraine is unlikely to experience significant setbacks on the battlefield.What Zelensky calls his "long-range sanctions" campaign against Russia is in full swing, causing mounting damage to the Russian economy. Ukraine's long front lines, meanwhile, remain largely static, thanks to a 15-30km (9-18-mile) wide "kill zone" where anything or anyone who moves is observed and attacked by drones.As a young, still relatively immature democracy, Ukraine's institutions have been put under colossal strain by Russia's full-scale invasion. But, many argue, the country remains resilient and resourceful."The secret of Ukraine's success is that we are much stronger horizontally than vertically," opposition MP Andrii Osadchuk told me."I hope the damage will be minimal."

schema.headline: Ukraine's Zelensky struggles to fix crisis over removal of defence minister Fedorov

title: Tottenham players not 'happy' and 'proud' to stay should leave - Roberto de Zerbi
description: Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi says players who are not happy at the club this summer should move elsewhere.The Italian, who took over at Spurs at
body: Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi says players who are not happy at the club this summer should move elsewhere.The Italian, who took over at Spurs at the end of March and helped save them from Premier league relegation last season, made his comments amid doubts over Lucas Bergvall's future at the club.Tottenham rejected a first bid of £38m from Nottingham Forest for Sweden midfielder Bergvall, with Forest set to up their offer to £45m."I was very clear at the start of my time in Tottenham. I said, who doesn't want to stay in Tottenham? Who is not happy, is not proud to stay here, has to leave," De Zerbi said, external before his side's pre-season friendly against Auckland FC in New Zealand on Sunday (04:30 BST)."I want the players to be proud and happy to stay here, to go on the pitch in Tottenham Hotspur Stadium with big motivation. Because now in football, if you think also in the World Cup, the motivation makes the difference. "The motivation is to be happy to stay in one team."Bergvall, who joined Spurs from Swedish club Djurgarden in 2024, played limited minutes at the end of last season under De Zerbi.The 20-year-old started the Italian's first game in charge – a 1-0 defeat at Sunderland – and, after that, made four appearances as a substitute.Spurs have since signed midfielders Sandro Tonali - in a £100m deal from Newcastle United - and Mateus Fernandes for £85m from West Ham."I have not spoken with Lucas yet," said De Zerbi. "I will in the next days and we will make the best decision for the club, for Lucas, for me, for every one of us, without problems. Lucas is a big, big talent."There will be a big competition to play because at the end, I think we will be two players for each position. "If he wants to stay, I will be happy. Otherwise, we have to find a new solution with [sporting director] Johan Lange, with [chief executive] Vinai [Venkatesham]. It's not my business after the decision to leave."Tottenham have also added defenders Jan Paul van Hecke, Andy Robertson and Marcos Senesi to their ranks and De Zerbi says now the "target is to complete the attacking positions"."First of all, I think it's not finished yet, our transfer market window," he added. "We have to finish, we have to bring another couple of, maybe more, maybe not less, but a couple of players."Bergvall is part of Tottenham's squad in New Zealand but wingers Mohammed Kudus (thigh) and Dejan Kulusevski (knee) have not travelled as they recover from long-term injuries."Kudus is very close. I think when we come back to London he will be available to start working with us," said De Zerbi. "It's a great thing for us. Kudus is another important player."Kulusevski, we have to see in the next couple of weeks. He's another important player. After one season, one complete season, without a game, we have to analyse better and better, don't take risks, first of all for him and then for us."Meanwhile, Spurs attacking midfielder Xavi Simons said "the first four days were the worst days of my life" as he recalled the anterior cruciate ligament injury he suffered in April.The Netherlands international required surgery on the serious knee injury and missed the 2026 World Cup."I couldn't sleep, I didn't eat for one week," he told Tottenham's website. "I was in a lot of pain. I was vomiting and felt dizzy, it was everything. That pain, I don't wish no-one to go through that pain."I don't know what it's like for other players but, for me, it was like my whole body was saying like 'what happened?'"This is what it is. I'm happy and in a good place now."

schema.headline: Tottenham players not 'happy' and 'proud' to stay should leave - Roberto de Zerbi

title: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous? Your thoughts on wedding rule changes
description: Image source, KJA Photography/Kimberley AppletonImage caption, Courtney and Sam Scholey had their dream wedding day at a venue in the Oxfordshire coun
body: Image source, KJA Photography/Kimberley AppletonImage caption, Courtney and Sam Scholey had their dream wedding day at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside - only it wasn't legalByTiffanie TurnbullThe day Sam and Courtney Scholey became husband and wife didn't feel like their wedding day.There was no walking down the aisle, no rings exchanged, no wedding dress, and no music.That all came several days later, when the pair had a bespoke ceremony led by a celebrant who knew them, at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside. It was their dream wedding - but it wasn't legal in England and Wales.And so in April, they forked out hundreds of pounds to quietly sign papers at a library in Buckingham."For us, that day was as insignificant as possible,"  Courtney told the BBC. "It was just the words we had to say to make it legally binding."The Scholeys are one of a growing number of couples who feel the rigid rules around weddings are making getting married more stressful, more expensive and less meaningful.But under new proposals announced this month - described by the government as the biggest shake-up of wedding laws in 200 years - couples in England and Wales could have the freedom to hold official marriage ceremonies in a wider array of unconventional locations, from forests to beaches, as long as the location is approved by a registered officiant.It's welcome news for Nicky Brown, who said she wants to exchange vows in a wildly picturesque corner of Wales, with just her mum and her partner's mum as witnesses. "I'd be quite happy to get married in a field full of sheep," the 57-year-old told the BBC.But some say the sacred tradition of marriage is being perverted.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Wedding rules date back to the 18th and 19th CenturiesCurrently, a marriage or civil partnership ceremony in England or Wales must take place at an approved venue to be legally binding – and many exert control on elements of the wedding such as vows, headcounts or music.There are also tight restrictions on who can officiate a wedding and how. Authorised religious figures can, but – with few exceptions – only in places of worship. Registrars can conduct a wedding, but it can't have any religious content. And celebrants can't legally marry people at all.A Law Commission report in 2022 concluded that these marriage laws, which date back to the 18th and 19th Centuries, were "complicated, inefficient, unfair and needlessly restrictive".David Lammy, then deputy prime minister, said marriage laws in England and Wales had "not kept pace with the social and cultural changes that have shaped modern Britain".He added: "Some feel forced to pay for two different ceremonies, one legal and one belief based. Some enter into a marriage that isn't legally recognised. Others feel they have little choice but to marry in a way which doesn't reflect their beliefs, marring what should be a joyous occasion."Scotland and Northern Ireland relaxed their rules years ago. Though the exact shape of the new rules is still under public consultation until September, these changes will take regulations from a "buildings based" regulation model to an "officiant based" one.'The laws are now, what, 200 years out of date?'Brown said she and her partner had put off getting married because there was no legal and affordable version of a wedding that reflects them.She said she didn't want bells and whistles - or even a wedding dress. "I just want somebody to marry us and in a beautiful setting that isn't just going to cost the earth."Brown went on to explain that she'd been scared her mum - who is 86 and unwell - would miss out on her wedding day. But these proposals had given her hope: "The laws are now, what, 200 years out of date?"Miranda Allard, 66, agreed that change is long overdue.When she got married 40 years ago, she had to jump through hoops to get permission to hold an interfaith ceremony in her parent's garden - and finds it astounding couples today face the same obstacles."We applied for a special licence... [and] explained how we did not want to put my Jewish mother-in-law through a church wedding," she said."I, on the other hand, was brought up in a Christian family and would not 'feel married' if doing so in a registry office."It took letters from the couple, their parents, the local bishop, the village vicar and more to convince authorities to allow the ceremony."We also combined our legal Christian service with Jewish prayers and tradition, like breaking the glass. Totally unheard of then and ever since," she said, adding the nuptials even made the paper.Image source, Miranda AllardImage caption, Simon and Miranda Allard had to get permission to hold an interfaith ceremony in her parent's garden when they got married 40 years ago... Image source, Miranda AllardImage caption, ... their nuptials even made the paper Father John, who didn't provide his last name, wrote in to BBC Your Voice to say he'd like to be able to perform ceremonies like this too."Marriage is about the lifelong commitment made before God for me, and for some couples the setting can make that sacred moment even more personal and memorable."Brian Bracher, 65, from Chichester in West Sussex, said he cannot believe the UK is still debating these changes."It is ridiculous that, in this modern era, a small minority are still trying to exert control and make decisions about what is frivolous and not acceptable. Just let people, that love each other, marry in a way that suits them."The proposals will be a welcome change for Christians from the LGBT community, said 33-year-old Isabel Sinagola. She added: "[They] currently cannot have the wedding they might want, as they cannot marry in the Church of England, but also cannot have religious content in the only option available to them: a civil ceremony." Others are hopeful this provides more affordable wedding options.'We want to get married but won't, as it costs too much'Carl Jones said he and his partner of 20 years haven't wed because even the simplest weddings are too expensive."We want to get married but won't, as it costs too much. It's cheaper if we just have two witnesses, but why should our [12-year-old] daughter not be allowed to attend... It's wrong."But sceptics say this will do little to lower the cost of weddings, which according to wedding planner app Hitched has jumped to £21,990 on average.Reverend Tom Kennar said it isn't marriage that is expensive, it's the extras most modern couples like to add."[It] is the costs of the reception, vehicles, booze, photographers, clothing, food, cars etc," he said.Other critics of the proposal say they fear it will dilute the significance of marriage."Marriage is a gift from God to secure society. Not an opportunity to set new standards and styles," said Donald Tosh, from Glasgow, who wrote to BBC Your Voice."It's now not a life decision, it's a temporary decision. And now with this, a very temporary frivolous decision," said Oliver, from Kent.However, celebrant Zadie Ward told the BBC the changes could enhance the meaning of a wedding for many couples."[Critics] are saying it's a solemn promise and it's about the serious commitment, but how can you ask someone to make a serious commitment in words that mean nothing to them and ways that are meaningless to them?"Image source, Sophie Ann PhotographyImage caption, "Modern relationships deserve modern ceremonies," says celebrant Zadie Ward She says the changes won't take anything from those who still want traditional weddings – it simply gives couples who don't more options."You've got blended families, mixed cultures, traditions that are changing even within those cultures. "Modern relationships deserve modern ceremonies."The government has stressed there will be safeguards to guarantee the dignity of marriage is preserved.Ceremonies deemed to be "gimmicks" that risk trivialising the legal act of marriage would not be allowed. Activities "such as skydiving, white-water rafting, roller coasters or other amusement rides" would "fall short of the standard"."Every couple deserves to start their journey together with an unforgettable day that reflects their beliefs, their personalities and the lives they plan to build together," Lammy wrote."This Government's changes will bring weddings law into the twenty-first century."Additional reporting by Mary Litchfield and Rozina Sini

schema.headline: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous? Your thoughts on wedding rule changes

title: Daizen Maeda: Ipswich sign Japan forward from Celtic
description: Ipswich Town have signed Japan forward Daizen Maeda from Celtic on a three-year contract.The 28-year-old, who has joined the Premier League side in a
body: Ipswich Town have signed Japan forward Daizen Maeda from Celtic on a three-year contract.The 28-year-old, who has joined the Premier League side in a reported £10m deal,, external was part of his country's squad at the 2026 World Cup and helped them reach the last 32 before they were knocked out by Brazil.Maeda scored 79 goals in 212 appearances at Celtic, where he won five league titles, three Scottish Cups and two League cups."I have always dreamed of playing in the Premier League and I am very happy I can realise that dream with this club," Maeda told Ipswich's website., external"I have loved all of the conversations with the club and they have made me feel very welcome."My aim will always be to battle hard, score goals, and provide assists for my team - I will always run and give everything that I have."Ipswich manager Gary O'Neil, who took over at Portman Road in the summer following the departure of Kieran McKenna, believes Maeda will be "a valuable member" of his squad.Maeda joins the Tractor Boys following their promotion back into the top flight after they finished second in the Championship under McKenna last season. "He works extremely hard and has impressive physical attributes, while also proving over a number of years playing in Scotland that he has the ability to score goals and create for his team," said O'Neil.Ipswich have added Maeda to the arrivals of defender Issa Diop, winger Abdul Fatawu, striker Emersonn and goalkeeper Kayne van Oevelen.In addition, defender Cedric Kipre and forward Chuba Akpom signed on a permanent basis following successful loans last season.In a social media post, external to the "Celtic family", Maeda said "the last four and a half years at Celtic have been the most special chapter of my career and my life".He added: "It has been an incredible honour to wear this badge, to play for this amazing club, and to share so many unforgettable moments with my teammates, the staff, and the best supporters in the world."Thank you for standing by me through every high and low."When Maeda joined Celtic as a relatively unknown J-League attacker in 2022, no one could have imagined the kind of success he would go on to have at the club.Maeda arrived in the early days of the Ange Postecoglou era, making the switch from Yokohoma F Marinos to Glasgow initially on loan in late December 2022 before completing a permanent switch in the following summer.His pace and energy has helped Celtic on numerous occasions but the 2025-26 campaign is what he will be most fondly remembered for.After failing to replace Kyogo Furuhashi up front, Celtic relied on Maeda to play through the middle for almost the entirety of last season.Having initially struggled for form, he turned things around when it mattered most.Maeda was on a barren run of just one goal in 18 games and Celtic were second in the table, trailing league leaders Hearts.What followed was transformational. Maeda scored seven goals in five Premiership matches, two of which were game winners.He scored the unforgettable second goal in the final-day decider at home to Hearts when, with the score level at 1-1, Maeda fired beyond Alexander Schwolow on 87 minutes to send Celtic Park wild.In his final game for Celtic, Maeda opened the scoring in a comfortable Scottish Cup final win over Dunfermline Athletic.While many fans will be sad to see him go, they probably feel it is a deserved move for a player that has contributed so much."His relentless energy and vital goals were an essential part of the team over the past four-and-a-half years, and he was a firm favourite with Celtic fans," said a Celtic statement., external"As he heads on to pastures new at Ipswich Town, everyone at Celtic thanks Daizen for his contribution to the club over the past few years and we wish him all the best for the future."

schema.headline: Daizen Maeda: Ipswich sign Japan forward from Celtic

title: Fleeing a wall of flames: Tourists describe France wildfires escape
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Evacuation efforts are underway in south-west FranceByEwan SomervilleFamilies have relived how their
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Evacuation efforts are underway in south-west FranceByEwan SomervilleFamilies have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".Image source, Andrea GrettonImage caption, A family showed the BBC how clouds of smoke descended on their campsite in Biscarrosse, south-west France"We had the gendarmerie [French military] going door to door," he told BBC Your Voice. "It was something like out of a movie - we had to take everything."Since experiencing "panic" before a "well organised" operation to clear out the entire peninsula, he said he received four different evacuation alerts from the authorities - the most recent at 17:00 on Friday - after "we moved away from one fire to only get put into the crosshairs of another".His family took shelter on a beach in nearby Arcachon before a relative came to their aid with a place to stay. His brother Nate, 11,  is still coming to terms with having seen the flames."Other people have been sleeping in schools and warehouses and the beaches have had people just waiting for the go ahead," Morrison added. "There's people on the beach here with their suitcases."He said the family was awaiting instructions on whether they can continue their holiday until mid August."It rained last night but we are hearing that electricity may be cut out over the peninsula, especially as the ash clouds go towards Bordeaux... I've heard about houses burning in just an hour, it's scary but sadly people here are getting used to it."Family fled in 15 minutesImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The wildfire on Moutchic beach on the shore of Lake LacanauDavid Morton had enjoyed most of his week-long trip to Cap Ferret with his wife and two teenage sons in the forests under baking sun. But the mixture of "tinder dry" pine and intense heat helped upend things on day five when the family was awoken on Friday morning."Our phones were all flashing and bleeping; there was a message saying we had to evacuate immediately and drive on the one road out of the [Cap Ferret] peninsula," he said."We literally threw everything into our suitcases and within 15 minutes were in the hire car."He said they came within 500m of the main fire. "The flames were higher than full-size forest pine trees, so five or six storeys high, and it was clear this was a fire that was out of control at that point."The family has stayed with friends until their flight home from Bordeaux on Saturday.Image source, David MortonImage caption, David Morton's holiday was going smoothly until the final two days'City is evacuated but I'm still here'Others are still stranded. Rebecca Papin, a French-American visiting her holiday home in the commune of Biscarrosse, near to the Cap Ferret peninsula, saw a large plume of smoke in the distance on Thursday.Just three hours later when she arrived home that night, "there were water planes in the sky dropping water, firefighter helicopters in the sky and the entire distance was just a wall of flames," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme."It was quite far away from my house but I could see it very clearly from the upstairs level of my home."She said the authorities appeared "overwhelmed with trying" to fight the fire and issued no evacuation order, so she slept alongside her young children with her earplugs in - meaning she missed the sound of the evacuation overnight.Image source, David MortonImage caption, The flames seen from David Morton's car window"When I woke up in the morning we were almost alone in the city because the city has been evacuated and I'm still here," she said."The main roads are closed because they're on fire - the police advised me on Friday at 07:30 to stay in my home, to not leave my home under any circumstance; there was ash falling from the sky like snow."Some British families told the BBC they had moved 100 miles away to other parts of France to continue their holidays.Mark Dorey, from Leeds, decided to drive to the Dordogne with his wife and three children after being evacuated from a campsite near Parentis-en-Born."You wouldn't believe it, but me and my two boys were watching a Queen tribute act at the campsite bar - straight after a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody someone stopped them to say we were being evacuated at about 22:00," he said.Before heading to the Dordogne the family spent a night with hundreds of other evacuees in a gymnasium. Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Shelters have been set up for evacuated residents and holidaymakersHe said he feels lucky to be looked after and safe, but is thinking about holidaying "closer to home" next year.And BBC South's Joanna Kent, who was on holiday in the Cap Ferret peninsula earlier this week, recalled seeing her campsite deserted after two van loads of police told tourists they had 30 minutes to get out.While the wildfires show no sign of abating soon, the UK Foreign Office is currently not advising against travel to France or Spain.Éléonore Caroit, France's minister for international partnerships, advised tourists on Saturday: "You have entire areas that are fine, you're seeing similar phenomena in Spain and other countries."I'm in Paris and nothing is happening, and most other regions are OK, so do please come to France and do not cancel your travel plans."But wherever you are, please do be advised as to what might be happening."In Madrid the fires are in the wider region far outside the city centre - and authorities are battling to stop different fires merging.But the flames have already shut down a facility for US space agency Nasa 37 miles (65km) west of the city.Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the fire there as the "worst fire in the history of the region", with the area facing a "perfect storm" of high temperatures, relentless wind and merging fire fronts.

schema.headline: Fleeing a wall of flames: Tourists describe France wildfires escape

title: 'The dogs were getting upset': How LA band Muna survived their worst ever gig
description: The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenasImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's concert for rescue dogs didn't
body: The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenasImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's concert for rescue dogs didn't go according to planByMusic correspondentEvery band has to earn its stripes. Some have it harder than others.At AC/DC's first gig, the club owner cut the power because they were too noisy. Sam Smith started at barn dances, singing on top of a haystack. At Robert Smith's first concert, he got so drunk that he sang David Bowie's Suffragette City while the rest of the band played Jimi Hendrix's Foxy Lady.But LA pop trio Muna can top them all.At the start of their career, the band got a call from their record label. We know you've just flown overnight from London, they said, but you have to get to Las Vegas.Why? Because they'd been booked to play Pet-A-Palooza, a dog adoption festival sponsored by the local radio station. If they turned up, the station would support their new single."We were all sick, so it was doomed from the start," recalls guitarist Josette Maskin."It was an acoustic set, but we didn't have a sound guy, and the guitar started feeding back."The noise, according to singer Katie Gavin, was like an unholy screech."The dogs were getting upset," says Maskin, wincing at the memory. "They just howled the whole time."We were mortified, but looking back, it is so funny. And I've gotten to share those experiences with some of my best friends, and that's what life is really about."Image source, Dean BradshawImage caption, Muna in 2026 (L-R): Naomi McPherson, Katie Gavin and Josette MaskinNowadays, that canine catastrophe is a dot in Muna's rear-view mirror. Over the past decade, they've become one of the most compelling live bands around – a little bit punk, a little bit electronic, a little bit 80s, eminently watchable and endlessly impressive.Fans include Harry Styles and Taylor Swift, who handpicked the trio (completed by guitarist/producer Naomi McPherson) to support them on tour.They were won over by sing-along anthems like I Know A Place, a great big exuberant hug for the LGBTQ community; and the more introspective Stayaway, where Gavin locks herself in her bedroom to avoid anything - friends, music, drink - that could tempt her back into the arms of an ex.In 2020, all their momentum nearly came to a crashing halt when RCA Records dropped the band, citing pandemic-era cost-cutting."That's obviously one where we had to put our heads together and be like, 'OK, we want to continue doing this. Let's just make an album and we'll figure it out'," says McPherson.'We need movement'That album, simply titled Muna, was eventually released by indie star Phoebe Bridgers, who swooped in to sign the band to her Saddest Factory label in 2021."Phoebe's manager had made it very clear that if we were ever single, she'd be interested in working with us," Gavin told the BBC at the time.Bridgers also provided guest vocals on Silk Chiffon, a freewheeling sapphic love song that became Muna's breakthrough single.It pegged the band, in its members' own words, as "the queer joy mini-skirt rollerblade, external" crew - but their music has always dug deeper than that.I Know A Place, for example, was written as a response to the 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting, acknowledging the fragility of the communal LGBTQ spaces it celebrated.Their fourth album, Dancing On The Wall, is their most powerful yet.The music is darker. The lyrics hit harder. Ostensibly anchored to the dancefloor, it's a record that uses dance music to shake the listener out of complacency."I think it was a response to a feeling of helplessness in this moment in time that can lead to paralysis," says Gavin."Movement is what we need right now, and we also need to feel powerful and to connect to our sources of energy. The tempo of this album helps with that."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The band are best seen live: "We were super lucky to hit at the right time to be able to play tiny venues and work our way up to where we are now," says McPhersonThe standout, lyrically speaking, is Big Stick. A critique of American imperialism, it's written from the perspective of Big Brother, who "can make you want anything that I want you to" – from war in Gaza to the militarisation of US police forces."And If you've got a problem with it, you could end up in jail," Gavin seethes as militaristic synths patrol the beat."I think sometimes people want to go to concerts to feel a brief reprieve from the horrors of the world around them, but right now the horrors are so pervasive that what I found myself wanting was a container to express my anger together with other people," says the singer."It's an emotional release that I think we are often denied because we have to read tragedies in the news every day and then keep our heads down and work."Given the polarised state of political discourse in the US, did they have any misgivings about releasing the song?"Maybe this is actually stupid, but I don't think it was a big decision for us," says Maskin."We have always been a political band, and we've always been super open with what we believe in, so it really wasn't a question."Elsewhere, the album transports the listener to sweaty, laser-lit nightclubs, where unyielding rhythms fuel feelings of "horniness and heartache".The title track is full of thwarted desire, as Gavin tries and fails to get the attention of a girl who constantly leaves her dangling. Wannabeher, meanwhile, is a sticky, sleazy track about being so completely besotted with someone that you start to blur the boundaries between where your personality ends and theirs begins."I think that's a canon gay experience, where you don't know whether you want to be with someone or you actually want to be them," laughs Maskin.Image caption, The band formed at university in 2013, with McPherson producing all of their musicEastside Girls, meanwhile, is a tender depiction of Muna's neighbourhood, lovingly lampooning the staples of LA hipster culture – astrology, polyamory, roommate dramas and "negronis with the nice gin"."It's a city that's run by sunshine," says McPherson, who moved to LA from her native San Diego."It's bohemian but it's also populated by some of the richest people in the world. It's a strange dichotomy."The song's chorus is a masterclass in melody and, in Maskin's words, "smacks you in the face". It takes its place among Muna's most irresistible hooks (see also, Number One Fan, Stayaway, What I Want) – which all stem from Gavin's love of classic pop."She's been writing songs since she was eight years old, so it's a well-honed skill," says McPherson."I think it's a benefit of my obsessive personality, honestly," says Gavin."I am constantly searching for the next big chorus, and will probably always be. Also, once I have a seed in my head for a song that feels promising, it really has a hold on me and won't let me go until I feel I've done it justice." (Wannabeher, McPherson reveals, is the final version of a song that began 11 years ago.)"I will say," Gavin adds, "one random tip is writing in motion - walking, driving, rollerblading, anything like that."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's tour hits the UK this November, in their biggest venues to dateThat explains why Muna's music always feels propulsive. "If you're not sweating after the first song, come on," laughs McPherson.With an ever-growing fanbase, they'll play their biggest ever tour this autumn, titled the Gets So Hot Tour after the album's opening track – although the band previously joked it would be called "The Midwest Princess, Midnight Sun and the Eras Tour as Well", before abandoning the idea for copyright reasons.A decade into their career, they're playing to "crowds we could never have imagined", while witnessing the genre labelled as "queer pop" expand into the mainstream, with artists like Chappell Roan, Renée Rapp, Lil Nas X and Troye Sivan all achieving crossover success."I do feel we were at the cusp of the reclamation of the word 'queer'," says Maskin."To us, it's actually a celebratory term, because it's inclusive, it includes everybody in the LGBTQI+ community."It came from academia first, the idea of queer theory," says McPherson, who admits the band were initially divided on whether to be open about their sexuality."We were reticent to come out of the closet in the hipster Pitchfork era of 2010 and 2011. We wanted to be mysterious and be closeted, and Katie was the one who encouraged us not to, and to just be ourselves. And we've only become more ourselves."Even so, the label can be restrictive. Muna want their music to be universal."The subject matter we write about is queer in its essence, and so are our life experiences," says McPherson."The issue that we struggle with is wanting that to also be accepted as just a human experience, as well – especially in these times of great repression."If anyone can do it, Muna can. Just don't let them play for your pets.

schema.headline: 'The dogs were getting upset': How LA band Muna survived their worst ever gig

title: BuzzBallz are 'greenwashing' say recycling experts
description: BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.BuzzBallz's UK's mission statem
body: BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.BuzzBallz's UK's mission statement, which was deleted after the BBC contacted the company about this story, said it "loves our planet as much as we love a good cocktail" and partnered with TerraCycle to ensure its packaging gets recycled. However, TerraCycle, which involves consumers collecting packaging and sending it to be recycled, only runs the BuzzBallz scheme in the United States. BuzzBallz's UK FAQs, now also deleted, stated: "Yes, our packaging is recyclable. Please recycle your empties where local facilities allow."But no local facilities anywhere in the UK allow BuzzBallz to be recycled, said Adam Herriott, the head of packaging at WRAP."They're a mix of two very recyclable materials that put together makes an unrecyclable format."No local authorities will accept these at the kerbside."If they end up at a sorting facility, they could end up contaminating the plastic stream because of the metals in there and that could be very problematic for plastics recyclers that get into the machinery."But why should people care if their drink packaging is not recyclable?Even the shape of the BuzzBallz make it harder to be recycled because they can roll on the conveyor belts at the sorting facilities, said Herriott.  Among the machinery used, scanners can identify it in one position, but by the time air jets are used to separate it into the right recycling stream, it could have moved, meaning it could contaminate other streams. "It's definitely one of the villains of recycling," said Ambarish Mitra, co-founder of Greyparrot, a waste analytics company which helps recovery facilities. He said BuzzBallz have "have no recovery route in the current system" and "is a huge pet peeve for our customers and us".After analysing a plastic recover facility in Manchester with a processing capacity of 35,000 tonnes of plastic a year, for six months, the company found that BuzzBallz contaminated recycled plastic 66% of the time. "Once in the plastic stream, the aluminium reduces the quality of the recycled plastic, while the colour pigments can lower the recycled plastic bale's value."This isn't a recycling problem. It's a packaging problem."BuzzBallz refused to comment.James Piper, co-host of the Talking Rubbish podcast, co-owner of Ecosurety, said he dislikes BuzzBallz because of how difficult they are to recycle. "Every stage of the recycling journey has been designed around predictable packaging," Piper said. "When people come along and say, 'I'm going to make something different for marketing reasons', they are automatically making it more difficult for the recycler.""There's nothing environmentally positive about mixing packaging types."He said the BuzzBallz 'biggies' which have a plastic screw top lid is completely recyclable."Anyone can say on their website 'this is recyclable where your council allows'. But if no council allows it, then it doesn't mean anything," he said. BuzzBallz said: "We very recently went through a global website update and the information pertaining to TerraCycle recycling for BuzzBallz was incorrectly copied and does not apply to the UK market as of today. "We apologise for the oversight and have since updated our website to reflect the correct position for UK consumers."The company refused to comment on the now-deleted UK FAQs stating its packaging was recyclable.

title: CMN birthmark no barrier for young footballing TV star
description: The family of a teenage footballer born with a rare skin condition have spoken of their pride after he landed a role in CBBC show Jamie Johnson FC.Eth
body: The family of a teenage footballer born with a rare skin condition have spoken of their pride after he landed a role in CBBC show Jamie Johnson FC.Ethan, from York, has congenital melanocytic naevus (CMN), a genetic condition that can result in large birthmarks covering up to 80% of the body.However, his parents, Tom and Abbi, said the 14-year-old's birthmark had "never defined him" and that his achievements were a reflection of his "determination and strength".Jodi Whitehouse, from CMN charity Caring Matters Now, said: "Seeing Ethan on screen means so much, not only to our CMN community but to every young person who has ever felt different because of how they look."Ethan's new role saw him join the ranks of aspiring players at fictitious football academy Hawx United for season four of the show.He was selected to feature in the series while he was with York City FC Academy. His audition involved playing a football match against the TV show's existing actors to show off his skills, after which he was cast as a squad member.Executive producer Sam Talbot said Ethan's role on the series reflected "something that is hugely important to us as a show"."We want all children to see themselves represented on screen and to feel that they belong in the stories we tell," he said."Creating a world that reflects the diversity and individuality of our audience will always be at the heart of what we do."Although a non-speaking role, Ethan still got plenty of screen time and a few close-ups, which, for someone with no acting experience could be surreal, he said"It was the first time, it was all pretty much new to me," he said, adding the main issue was keeping a straight face and not laughing.Representing those with visible skin differences "never really crossed his mind" - for him, the focus has always been playing football.Tom and Abbi said they "couldn't be prouder" of their son.His stint on TV, alongside his burgeoning football career, has helped with "confidence building", according to them."He's just is who he is," Abbi said."I think just getting out there, people are accepting of it. Everyone we know just treats Ethan as Ethan."With filming finished and the series now available to watch on BBC iPlayer, the teen is turning his attention back to his beloved sport.However, he said he'd "definitely go [back] for another" season of the show."It was really fun and I enjoyed all of it," he said.

schema.headline: CMN birthmark no barrier for young footballing TV star

title: Police declare 'major incident' over Nethy Bridge wildfire
description: Figure caption, A change in the wind direction caused a flare-up on Thursday night Updated 1 minute agoA major incident has been declared by emergency
body: Figure caption, A change in the wind direction caused a flare-up on Thursday night Updated 1 minute agoA major incident has been declared by emergency services as they continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Park for 10 days.Some residents of the village of Nethy Bridge have been evacuated as a precaution. But a local resident told the BBC the wildfire should have been declared a major incident sooner and communication from authorities had been "pretty poor".The Scottish government said a fire break had been established around Nethy Bridge overnight and new fire breaks were being constructed.First Minister John Swinney, who held a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience committee early on Saturday, said additional police and fire service resources were being deployed to assist with the evacuation. He said that it was "essential people avoid the affected areas."Swinney continued: "The wind has changed direction overnight, which means the track of the fire has altered once again and the threat to Nethy Bridge has reduced, for the moment at least. "Ground and helicopter resources are being focused on the current path of the fire and new fire breaks constructed."Smoke from the wildfire can now be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen following a change in wind direction.Image source, JasperImageImage caption, The risk of the fire spreading has changed with the weather The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said people living in properties north-west of Dorback Lodge at Lain Thatchan had been also been evacuated and advised people living in Tomintoul to keep windows and doors closed due to smoke.Police Scotland said the major incident had been declared and the decision to evacuate residents taken came after evidence on Friday night suggested the fire was spreading towards Nethy Bridge.A spokesperson added that residents were being directed to a dedicated respite centre at the Macdonald Aviemore Hotel and access roads into the village had been closed. 'The horse has bolted' Richard Eccles and his wife Patricia run a guest house in the village.Eccles said on 22:00 on Friday night, police came to the door and gave them three options: stay, seek accommodation with family or friends elsewhere, or go to the emergency accommodation at the Macdonald hotel in Aviemore.Image caption, A dedicated respite centre has been set up at the Macdonald Aviemore HotelHe said they decided to stay unless the fire got considerably closer, adding: "We've got a camper van and we're all ready and set to go at a moment's notice. If it gets smoky, we'll go."A wedding was due to take place at Castle Roy, which is near the village, but Eccles said this has had to be cancelled as a result of the wildfire evacuations.He said the Scottish government's response had been "poor" and a major incident should have been declared earlier, with military assistance brought in to tackle the fire before it spread.Eccles said: "It's a bit like closing the stable door now that the horse has bolted."Image caption, Local resident John McGlinchey said he felt disappointed that residents were having to relocate at short noticeLocal resident John McGlinchey said he felt disappointed that residents were "having to wait until the flames are almost on our doorstep and having to relocate at such notice".He said there is a major concern for mobilising the many elderly people in the village and those with disabilities.With the "last-minute" evacuation call, a lot of people will also have to go out of pocket for accommodation because of a lack of contingency plans from the government, he added.Get in touchHave you been affected by the wildfire in the Cairngorms? MP for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine Andrew Bowie, who is the Conservative shadow secretary of state for Scotland, said "increasing numbers of constituents" had been getting in touch to express concern.In a letter, external to Scottish government minister Gillian Martin he claimed the SNP-led administration had "failed to treat the situation with the seriousness and attention that it deserves".He singled out the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service's (SFRS) lack of direct access to helicopter support. Currently it calls in private companies with helicopters and specialist equipment when needed.The SFRS has said the Cairngorms wildfire has been "appropriately resourced" from the start.Image source, Ronan DuganImage caption, New pockets or fires are still breaking out within the national parkMore than 100 firefighters have been tackling the blaze, which first broke out near Ryvoan Bothy, south of Nethy Bridge, last Wednesday.It covered an area of about six sq km (2.3 sq miles) of heather and small trees at its height.Eleven fire engines, wildlife units and a command support unit are still at the scene.Firefighters said miles-long firebreaks had helped to contain the latest break-outs on Thursday night while drones were directing crews to hot spots.Image source, JasperImageImage caption, Police officers on the scene are directing evacuated Nethy Bridge residents to an Aviemore hotelThe Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said the fire remained "dynamic and unpredictable".A spokesman said: "Changing wind strength and direction can cause flare-ups, reignition and the spread of smoke, with conditions continuing to evolve."Firefighters remain deployed to tackle the incident across a vast and complex landscape, supported by ongoing helicopter water-bombing operations," the SFRS spokesman added.Image caption, The wildfire in the Cairngorms has brought a haze to AberdeenThe SFRS had previously said residents and businesses in the east area of Aviemore, as well as across parts of Aberdeenshire - including Inverurie, Banchory and Kintore and surrounding areas - and as far as Aberdeen city, may see or smell smoke on Friday and into the weekend.They advised anyone affected to keep windows and doors closed.

schema.headline: Police declare 'major incident' over Nethy Bridge wildfire

title: Ormskirk restaurants save day after wedding catering no-show
description: A couple have praised staff at three restaurants that stepped in to save the day when they were let down by wedding caterers at the last minute.Kate a
body: A couple have praised staff at three restaurants that stepped in to save the day when they were let down by wedding caterers at the last minute.Kate and Matt Dean from Skelmersdale, Lancashire, were preparing to celebrate their wedding with family and friends at a venue in Ormskirk when the caterers failed to turn up and they were unable to get in touch with them.With guests starting to arrive, Kate said they decided to ask two local restaurants if they could help.Kate said she first approached restaurant staff at Piri Piri Grill, saying: "Hi! I don't suppose you can cook for 100 people?" and "he just went, 'oh, when?'... and I went, 'now'".The couple, who have four children aged two to 12 between them, were married at Ormskirk Register Office on 13 July.They decided to organise a special celebration for family and friends at Lost and Found Ormskirk on Sunday and were looking forward to the food arriving.They arrived at the venue two hours ahead of time to get it ready but when time was ticking on - with no sign of the caterers - their concern grew.They tried to call and message the business but there was no response and despite initially feeling upset - including crying in the bathroom at one point - Kate quickly hatched a back-up plan."I'm quite a laid back person anyway, so I was in fire-fighting mode, like we have got all these people coming and no food, 'what are we going to do?'," she said.Kate said when guests started arriving she thought about local venues she liked. "I just turned to Matt's family and said, 'if I can sort this, is everybody OK?'"The 32-year-old nail technician said they had been planning their wedding since September, after postman Matt, 36, proposed in 2022.She said the couple approached the teams at Piri Piri Grill and also at Scoozi Pizza and Pasta in Ormskirk and were hugely relieved when they agreed to help out.Despite both restaurants being busy with the World Cup final on that day, they insisted on closing to the public and devoting themselves to helping out the newlyweds, she added.Kate said it was great to see "towers of pizza boxes" which were "taller than Matt and he is 5ft 9ins (1.8m)".Meanwhile, staff at the Lost and Found venue in Ormskirk were "more than accommodating" and "so helpful" in working to ensure the change of plan ran smoothly, she said.Kate said the restaurant staff "were so amazing" and came back later on to check that everything was fine.She said that despite having "ended up crying in the bathroom" at one point, they could see the funny side to what happened as they looked back on the photos."It ended up being quite funny - it was kind of like the wedding story."Their children enjoyed "going around like little waiters with like four pizza boxes" with one saying "you ordered a pizza", she said.

schema.headline: Ormskirk restaurants save day after wedding catering no-show
